questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: A.4 (Rigid body mechanics: moment of inertia, rotational dynamics, rolling without slipping)
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.challenge_mechanism: Every key is reachable only by keeping the rolling constraint and the changing moment of inertia in play; each distractor is what remains once one of those two ideas is quietly dropped.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions on rigid-body mechanics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-2}}$ where a numerical value is needed, and give each answer to three significant figures.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A solid cylinder and a thin-walled hollow cylinder have the same mass and the same outer radius. Both are released from rest and roll without slipping down the same incline. What is the ratio of the acceleration of the solid cylinder to the acceleration of the hollow cylinder?

options.label: A
options.rationale: For rolling without slipping the acceleration is g sin theta divided by one plus I over M R squared, giving two thirds for the solid cylinder and one half for the hollow one, and the ratio of those is four thirds.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This inverts the ratio, comparing the hollow cylinder with the solid one rather than the other way round.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This treats every rolling body as accelerating alike, which is only true for sliding without friction and ignores where the energy goes.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This takes the ratio of the two moments of inertia directly, forgetting the leading term of one in the rolling acceleration formula.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A disc of moment of inertia $0.80\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{2}}$ rotates freely about a fixed vertical axle at $12\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. A lump of clay of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$, initially at rest, is dropped onto the disc and sticks at a point $0.60\ \mathrm{m}$ from the axle. What is the angular speed immediately afterwards?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Angular momentum about the axle is conserved at 9.6 units, the clay contributes m r squared of 0.18 to the moment of inertia, and dividing gives 9.6 over 0.98.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This assumes the angular speed is unchanged, which would only follow if the clay landed exactly on the axle and added nothing to the moment of inertia.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the angular momentum itself quoted as if it were an angular speed, a confusion of a conserved quantity with the quantity being found.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This adds m r rather than m r squared when increasing the moment of inertia, so the clay is treated as if it sat at unit distance.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A solid cylinder is released from rest on a rough incline and rolls down it without slipping, accelerating as it goes. What is the direction of the static frictional force that the surface of the incline exerts on the cylinder?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Weight and the normal force both give no torque about the centre of mass, so only friction can supply the torque that increases the spin, and it must point up the plane to do so.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This applies friction opposing motion rather than friction opposing the relative motion at the contact point, which is the condition static friction actually enforces.

options.label: C
options.text: Zero, because the cylinder does not slip
options.rationale: No slipping means no kinetic friction, but static friction is present and is precisely what produces the angular acceleration of the cylinder.

options.label: D
options.text: Perpendicular to the surface of the incline
options.rationale: This is the direction of the normal contact force, which passes through the centre and so cannot produce any torque about it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A light inextensible string is wound around a disc of radius $0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ whose moment of inertia about its axle is $0.30\ \mathrm{kg\ m^{2}}$. The disc turns on a fixed horizontal axle with negligible friction, and a block of mass $1.2\ \mathrm{kg}$ hangs from the free end of the string. What is the tension in the string as the block descends?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The tension torque spins the disc, so T equals I a over R squared, and combining with m g minus T equals m a gives an acceleration of 1.96 and hence a tension of 9.42 newtons.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This sets the tension equal to the weight of the block, which would mean zero acceleration and ignores that some energy goes into rotating the disc.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This is the resultant force on the block rather than the tension, having subtracted the tension from the weight instead of reporting it.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This substitutes the hanging block's own mass into the disc's moment of inertia, treating the disc as if it were a solid cylinder of that mass.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A solid uniform sphere of moment of inertia $\frac{2}{5}MR^2$ about its centre rolls without slipping along level ground at a constant speed of $3.0\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$. What fraction of the sphere's total kinetic energy is rotational kinetic energy?

options.label: A
options.rationale: With omega equal to v over R the rotational energy is one fifth M v squared while the translational energy is one half M v squared, so the rotational share is two sevenths.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This quotes the coefficient two fifths from the moment of inertia as if it were already the energy fraction, skipping the conversion entirely.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This assumes the energy splits equally between translation and rotation, which happens for no standard rolling body.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the translational fraction rather than the rotational one, obtained by taking the complement and so answering the question that was not asked.

questions.answer:
**(a)** For rolling without slipping the acceleration down an incline is $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/(MR^2)}$. The solid cylinder has $I = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$ and so accelerates at $\tfrac{2}{3}g\sin\theta$; the thin-walled hollow cylinder has $I = MR^2$ and so accelerates at $\tfrac{1}{2}g\sin\theta$. The ratio is $\tfrac{2/3}{1/2} = \tfrac{4}{3} = 1.33$. **(A1)** Option B inverts it, option C assumes every rolling body behaves the same, and option D takes the ratio of the moments of inertia without the denominator.

**(b)** Angular momentum about the axle is conserved, because neither the axle force nor the weight of the clay exerts a torque about it. Initially $L = 0.80 \times 12 = 9.6\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2\ s^{-1}}$. The clay contributes $mr^2 = 0.50 \times 0.60^2 = 0.18\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2}$, so the final moment of inertia is $0.98\ \mathrm{kg\ m^2}$ and the final angular speed is $9.6/0.98 = 9.80\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. **(A1)** Option B ignores the clay, option C reports the angular momentum as though it were a speed, and option D adds $mr$ instead of $mr^2$.

**(c)** The weight acts through the centre of mass and the normal force passes through the contact point, so neither produces a torque about the centre. Only friction can supply the torque that increases the angular speed, and it must act **up the incline** to do so. **(A1)** Note that static friction opposes the motion the contact point *would* have, not the motion of the centre of mass.

**(d)** The string does not slip, so $a = \alpha R$. Then $mg - T = ma$ for the block and $TR = I\alpha$ for the disc, giving $T = Ia/R^2$. Hence $a = \dfrac{mg}{m + I/R^2} = \dfrac{1.2 \times 9.81}{1.2 + 4.8} = 1.96\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-2}}$, and $T = 4.8 \times 1.96 = 9.42\ \mathrm{N}$. **(A1)** Option B neglects the disc's inertia, option C is the resultant force rather than the tension, and option D uses $I = \tfrac{1}{2}mR^2$ with the block's mass.

**(e)** With $I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2$ and $\omega = v/R$, the rotational term is $\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{5}Mv^2$ and the translational term is $\tfrac{1}{2}Mv^2$. The rotational fraction is therefore $\dfrac{1/5}{1/5 + 1/2} = \dfrac{2}{7} = 0.286$. **(A1)** Option B quotes the coefficient in $I$, option C splits the energy evenly, and option D is the translational fraction.
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark for each correct option. There is no penalty for a wrong answer under the Paper 1A rules, so every question should be attempted, and a student who cannot finish a calculation should eliminate on dimensional or limiting-case grounds and choose. In (a) condone the ratio written as $4:3$ or as $1.33$. In (b) allow follow-through from an incorrect final moment of inertia provided the conservation statement itself is explicit and correct. In (c) accept 'up the slope' or 'up the plane'; the direction must be given relative to the incline, and 'opposite to the motion' is not sufficient because the phrase is ambiguous here. In (d) accept $9.4\ \mathrm{N}$ to two significant figures, and allow an answer obtained by computing the acceleration first. In (e) accept $2/7$ or $0.29$; the fact that the answer has no unit is itself part of what is being assessed.  Candidates most often lose these marks not through algebra but by applying a purely translational model to a body that is also rotating; watch for a line of working in which the moment of inertia has quietly disappeared. A calculator is available throughout, so no credit is due for an unreduced surd where a decimal was requested, and values should carry three significant figures.
questions.explanation: What makes this cluster discriminate is that every distractor is the residue of a specific physical decision rather than of arithmetic noise. In (a) and (e) the trap is to treat a rolling body as a translating point mass: the moment of inertia enters twice, once through the dynamics and once through the energy, and dropping either occurrence produces options C and B respectively. In (b) the item is really asking whether you know that angular momentum, and not angular speed or rotational kinetic energy, is the quantity conserved when the moment of inertia changes. In (c) the popular wrong answer 'down the incline' comes from a half-remembered rule that friction opposes motion, when what friction opposes here is the relative motion at the contact point. In (d) the tension is not the weight because part of the released gravitational energy is going into spinning the disc; forgetting that gives option B, which is the single most common error in this subtopic.  A reliable check on any answer in this cluster is the limiting case: as the moment of inertia tends to zero the body must behave like a point mass moving freely, and every correct expression here reduces to that limit. A candidate who tests a result this way catches most of the traps the distractors set without redoing the algebra, which is why the habit is worth teaching explicitly.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. The distractor set for each item was built from the four error patterns that recur in this subtopic: dropping the rolling constraint, confusing a conserved quantity with the target, using r in place of r squared, and reporting the complement of the requested fraction.

verification.method: Every key and every distractor recomputed independently in Python to full precision, and each distractor confirmed to be the exact result of the named error rather than a nearby number.
solution_skeleton: identify the moment of inertia of each body from its geometry
apply the rolling constraint or conserve angular momentum about the axle
set up the rotational equation of motion together with the translational one
solve for the requested quantity and compare with the limiting case

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: D.4 (Induction: Faraday's law, Lenz's law, motional emf, self-inductance)
questions.challenge_mechanism: The items turn on whether the emf is written from the rate of change of flux rather than from the flux itself, and on whether charge is recognised as an integral of current over a transition rather than a net flux difference.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions on electromagnetic induction. Each one stands alone. In every case the magnetic field is uniform over the region stated and the resistance given is the total circuit resistance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A rectangular coil of 200 turns and resistance $4.0\ \Omega$ has one side of length $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ inside a uniform magnetic field of $0.80\ \mathrm{T}$. The coil is pulled out of the field at a constant speed of $0.20\ \mathrm{m\ s^{-1}}$, with that side remaining perpendicular to the direction of motion. What is the current in the coil while it leaves the field?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The emf is N B L v which is 1.6 volts, and dividing by the four ohm circuit resistance gives a current of 0.40 amperes.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the induced emf quoted as if it were the current, having omitted the division by the resistance of the circuit.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This uses the area of the coil where Faraday's law for a straight side needs the length, so an extra factor of the side appears.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This omits the number of turns entirely, computing the emf for a single loop and then dividing by the resistance.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A coil of 500 turns and area $0.020\ \mathrm{m^2}$ rotates at a steady frequency of $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in a uniform magnetic field of $0.10\ \mathrm{T}$, with its axis of rotation perpendicular to the field. What is the maximum emf induced across the coil?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The flux is N B A cos omega t so the emf is N B A omega sin omega t, and N B A omega with omega equal to two pi f gives 314 volts.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This uses pi f in place of two pi f for the angular frequency, halving the true peak emf.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This uses the frequency in hertz directly where the angular frequency in radians per second is required.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This is the maximum flux linkage N B A rather than its rate of change, describing the flux and not the emf at all.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An inductor of inductance $0.40\ \mathrm{H}$ carries a steady current of $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$. How much energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The stored energy is one half L I squared, which is one half times 0.40 times nine, giving 1.8 joules.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This omits the factor of one half, the same slip as using m v squared instead of one half m v squared for kinetic energy.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This computes L times I rather than L times I squared, treating the current as if it entered to the first power.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This halves L I rather than L I squared, applying the factor of one half to the wrong expression.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A square loop of side $0.10\ \mathrm{m}$ and resistance $2.0\ \Omega$ is pulled at constant speed completely through a region of uniform magnetic field of $0.50\ \mathrm{T}$ directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop. The region is wide enough that the loop enters and leaves separately. What total charge flows past a point in the loop?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Charge is the integral of current, which is the total change of flux linkage divided by the resistance, and the magnitudes on entry and on exit each contribute B a squared over R.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This counts only the entry transition and forgets that the loop leaves the field as well as entering it.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This argues from the net change in flux being zero, but charge is the integral of the current, so the two transitions add in magnitude rather than cancelling.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This uses twice the area of the loop in each transition, counting the field region as double the actual intercepted area.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A conducting rod of length $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ rotates at a steady angular speed of $20\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$ about one end, sweeping out a plane that is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $0.25\ \mathrm{T}$. What is the emf between the two ends of the rod?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Each element moves at a speed proportional to its distance from the pivot, so the mean speed is that of the midpoint and the emf is one half B omega L squared.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This treats every element of the rod as moving at the speed of the tip, omitting the factor of one half that comes from averaging along the rod.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This uses B omega L instead of B omega L squared, which is dimensionally wrong and gives a quantity that is not an emf.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This applies a factor of one half twice, once for the mean speed and then again without justification.

questions.answer:
**(a)** Only the side of length $L = 0.050\ \mathrm{m}$ that lies across the field boundary changes the flux, so $\varepsilon = NBLv = 200 \times 0.80 \times 0.050 \times 0.20 = 1.6\ \mathrm{V}$, and $I = \varepsilon/R = 1.6/4.0 = 0.40\ \mathrm{A}$. **(A1)** Option B reports the emf, option C puts the coil area where the side length belongs, and option D omits the turn count.

**(b)** The flux linkage is $N\Phi = NBA\cos(\omega t)$, so $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin(\omega t)$ with $\omega = 2\pi f = 314\ \mathrm{rad\ s^{-1}}$. Hence $\varepsilon_{\max} = 500 \times 0.10 \times 0.020 \times 314 = 314\ \mathrm{V}$. **(A1)** Option B uses $\pi f$ for $\omega$, option C uses $f$, and option D gives the flux linkage rather than its rate of change.

**(c)** $E = \tfrac{1}{2}LI^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.40 \times 3.0^2 = 1.80\ \mathrm{J}$. **(A1)** Option B omits the half, option C uses $LI$, and option D halves $LI$.

**(d)** The charge is $Q = \int I\,dt = \dfrac{1}{R}\int \varepsilon\,dt = \dfrac{|\Delta\Phi|}{R}$ over each transition. Entry gives $Ba^2/R = 0.50 \times 0.010/2.0 = 2.5\ \mathrm{mC}$ and exit gives the same again, so $Q = 5.0\ \mathrm{mC}$. **(A1)** This is the item that separates a student who has memorised a formula from one who knows what charge is: the *net* flux change over the whole motion is indeed zero, but the two currents flow at different times and it is their magnitudes, not their signs, that add.

**(e)** An element at distance $r$ moves at $\omega r$, so $d\varepsilon = B\omega r\,dr$ and $\varepsilon = \int_0^L B\omega r\,dr = \tfrac{1}{2}B\omega L^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.25 \times 20 \times 0.16 = 0.400\ \mathrm{V}$. **(A1)** Option B uses the tip speed throughout, option C is dimensionally inconsistent, and option D halves twice.
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per correct option, no negative marking. In (a) allow an answer reached via the rate of cutting of flux lines provided the length used is the one crossing the boundary. In (b) accept 314 V or 3.1 x 10^2 V, and condone a small discrepancy from rounding omega to 314. In (c) accept 1.8 J. In (d) do not credit an argument from the net flux change alone even if it reaches 5.0 mC by some other route, because the reasoning is what is being rewarded; equally, credit 5.0 mC reached by treating the two transitions separately as intended. In (e) accept 0.40 V and allow the integral form or the mean-speed argument.  Note that in (d) the speed at which the loop is pulled does not appear in the answer at all, and that is the point of the item: the charge depends only on the change of flux linkage and on the resistance. In (e) credit the integral form and the mean-speed argument equally, but do not credit B L v applied with the tip speed, which is precisely the error option B exists to catch. In (b) the value 314 V depends on using an angular frequency in radians per second; a candidate working in degrees will reach none of the options, which is a useful diagnostic in itself.
questions.explanation: The unifying idea is that an induced emf comes from a rate of change, never from a flux on its own, and that is what options D in (b), B in (a) and the whole of (d) are built to test. Item (d) is the hardest in the set and is the one that most reliably separates grade 6 from grade 7 candidates: the net change in flux linkage across the complete motion really is zero, and a candidate who has learned 'Q equals delta phi over R' without understanding that Q is a time integral will choose 0 mC with complete confidence. Item (e) rewards the same habit at the level of a single rod: because the speed varies along the rod, the emf has to be built up element by element, and the factor of one half is not a rule to remember but the result of that averaging. Across the cluster, dimensional checks eliminate at least one option in every item, which is the intended escape route for a candidate who runs short of time.  Items (a) and (e) are deliberately paired: both ask for an emf from a conductor moving in a magnetic field, and both are answered by B L v only when the whole conductor moves at the same speed, which is true in (a) and false in (e). Deciding which of the two situations applies is the transferable skill the cluster is built around, and it is the same decision that separates (d) from a naive use of the flux formula.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. Item (d) is written specifically against the 'net flux change is zero' reflex, and item (e) against the habit of quoting B L v without integrating along a rotating conductor.

verification.method: Each key and each distractor recomputed in Python to full precision; every distractor confirmed to be exactly the output of the error named in its rationale.
solution_skeleton: write Faraday's law with the flux expression appropriate to the geometry
evaluate the rate of change of flux for the stated motion
divide by the circuit resistance or integrate the current over the transition
check dimensions and match the magnitude to an option

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.syllabus_ref: B.5 (Current and circuits: internal resistance, non-ideal meters, power transfer)
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.challenge_mechanism: Every item turns on the circuit changing when the measuring instrument or the load is attached, so the idealised circuit diagram and the circuit that actually exists give different numbers.
questions.question: Five independent multiple-choice questions in which a circuit is altered by the act of measuring it, or by the load connected to it. In each case the supply is treated as ideal unless an internal resistance is stated explicitly.

parts.label: a
parts.text: A cell of emf $12\ \mathrm{V}$ and internal resistance $3.0\ \Omega$ is connected to a variable external resistor. What is the greatest power that can be dissipated in that external resistor?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Power is greatest when the load equals the internal resistance, giving a current of 2.0 amperes and hence I squared R of 12 watts.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is E squared over r, the power that would be dissipated inside the cell itself at short circuit rather than in the external load.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This uses E squared over two r, dropping the factor of four that comes from the load and the internal resistance both being in circuit.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This uses E squared over eight r, applying the maximum power result with an extra factor of two introduced without a reason.

parts.label: b
parts.text: For the cell in the previous question, at the external resistance that gives the greatest power in the external resistor, what fraction of the total power generated by the cell is delivered to that external resistor?

options.label: A
options.rationale: At maximum power the load equals the internal resistance, so equal power is dissipated in each and exactly half of what the cell generates reaches the load.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This ignores the internal resistance altogether, which is only valid for an ideal cell with no internal dissipation.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This corresponds to a load of twice the internal resistance, which delivers more than half the power but not the maximum possible power.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This corresponds to a load of one third of the internal resistance, where most of the generated power is lost inside the cell.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A cell of negligible internal resistance and emf $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$ is connected in series with a $400\ \Omega$ resistor and a $600\ \Omega$ resistor. A voltmeter of resistance $2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ is connected across the $600\ \Omega$ resistor. What does the voltmeter read?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The voltmeter and the 600 ohm resistor form a parallel pair of about 462 ohms, which then divides the 6.0 volts with the 400 ohm resistor to give 3.21 volts.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This treats the voltmeter as ideal with infinite resistance, ignoring the current it draws and the loading that results.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This combines the loaded resistance with the original unloaded total, changing one part of the circuit and not the other.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This puts the voltmeter across the 400 ohm resistor instead of the 600 ohm one, loading the wrong component of the potential divider.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A circuit consists of a $12\ \mathrm{V}$ supply of negligible internal resistance connected to a $100\ \Omega$ resistor. An ammeter of resistance $5.0\ \Omega$ is inserted in series to measure the current. What is the percentage error in the current it reads?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The true current is 0.12 amperes and the loaded current is 12 over 105, so the fractional error is the ammeter resistance over the new total of 105 ohms.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This uses the ammeter resistance over the original resistance alone, forgetting that adding the ammeter also increases the total resistance.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This assumes the ammeter is ideal and disturbs nothing, which is the approximation being tested rather than the situation described.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This reports the ratio of the measured current to the true one rather than the error, answering a different question with a correct calculation.

parts.label: e
parts.text: A cell is connected to a $4.0\ \Omega$ resistor and the terminal potential difference is $6.0\ \mathrm{V}$. When the same cell is connected to a $9.0\ \Omega$ resistor the terminal potential difference is $7.2\ \mathrm{V}$. What is the internal resistance of the cell?

options.label: A
options.rationale: The two loads draw 1.5 and 0.8 amperes, and the internal resistance is the change in terminal voltage divided by the change in current, giving 1.2 over 0.7.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This is the reciprocal of the correct value, obtained by dividing the change in current by the change in voltage.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This quotes the change in terminal voltage as though voltage were a resistance, without dividing by the change in current.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This gives the lost volts inside the cell for the first load rather than the resistance that produced them.

questions.answer:
**(a)** The power in the load is $P = \dfrac{E^2 R}{(R+r)^2}$, which is greatest when $R = r = 3.0\ \Omega$. Then $I = 12/6.0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and $P = I^2R = 4.0 \times 3.0 = 12\ \mathrm{W}$, which is also $E^2/(4r)$. **(A1)** Option B is $E^2/r$, the power dissipated inside the cell at short circuit, and options C and D come from dropping or doubling the factor of four.

**(b)** At $R = r$ the same current passes through both resistances, so $I^2R = I^2r$ and exactly **one half** of the generated power reaches the load. **(A1)** This is why maximum power transfer and high efficiency are different aims: option B needs an ideal cell, and options C and D correspond to $R = 2r$ and $R = r/3$ respectively.

**(c)** The voltmeter is in parallel with the $600\ \Omega$ resistor, giving $R_p = \dfrac{600 \times 2000}{2600} = 462\ \Omega$. The circuit total becomes $400 + 462 = 862\ \Omega$, so $I = 6.0/862 = 6.96\ \mathrm{mA}$ and the reading is $I R_p = 3.21\ \mathrm{V}$. **(A1)** Option B assumes an ideal meter, option C mixes the loaded resistance with the unloaded total, and option D loads the wrong resistor.

**(d)** True current $I_0 = 12/100 = 0.120\ \mathrm{A}$; with the ammeter in place $I = 12/105 = 0.1143\ \mathrm{A}$. The fractional error is $\dfrac{0.120 - 0.1143}{0.120} = 4.76\%$, which equals $R_A/(R + R_A) = 5.0/105$. **(A1)** Option B uses $R_A/R$, option C ignores the meter, and option D is the ratio of the two currents rather than the error.

**(e)** The currents are $I_1 = 6.0/4.0 = 1.5\ \mathrm{A}$ and $I_2 = 7.2/9.0 = 0.80\ \mathrm{A}$. Since $V = E - Ir$, subtracting gives $6.0 - 7.2 = -r(1.5 - 0.80)$, so $r = 1.2/0.70 = 1.71\ \Omega$ and $E = 8.57\ \mathrm{V}$. **(A1)** Option B inverts the gradient, option C quotes the voltage change, and option D quotes the lost volts.
questions.markscheme_notes: One mark per correct option, no negative marking. In (a) accept 12 W reached by differentiating the power expression or by quoting the maximum power theorem, provided the condition R equals r is stated. In (b) accept 50% or one half; note that a candidate who answers (a) correctly but (b) as two thirds has applied the theorem without understanding it. In (c) accept any value between 3.20 V and 3.22 V from premature rounding of the parallel pair. In (d) accept 4.8% to two significant figures, and credit the exact form 5/105. In (e) accept 1.7 ohms, and allow a graphical solution from a V against I plot provided the gradient is taken with the correct sign.  Across the cluster, a candidate who rounds the parallel resistance in (c) prematurely may report anything from 3.20 V to 3.22 V and should be credited; a comparable tolerance applies in (e). In (d) the exact form 5.0 over 105 earns the mark even when left as a fraction. Note that (a) and (b) are formally independent, so a candidate may answer either without the other, and no follow-through between them should be assumed either way.
questions.explanation: The whole cluster tests one idea that is easy to state and hard to hold on to under time pressure: connecting something to a circuit changes that circuit. In (c) and (d) the instrument is the thing that changes it, and the natural instinct to treat a voltmeter as invisible or an ammeter as free is exactly what options B and C are for. In (a) and (b) the load is the thing that changes it, and the pair together tests whether a candidate has memorised the maximum power theorem or understands it: knowing that maximum power occurs at R equals r is worth one mark, but knowing that this is also the point at which half the generated power is thrown away inside the cell is what distinguishes understanding from recall. Item (e) is the hardest to set up because neither the emf nor the internal resistance is given; the route in is to notice that the difference between the two terminal voltages is caused entirely by the difference between the two lost-volt terms, which turns a problem with two unknowns into a single subtraction.  The cluster also carries a lesson about experimental design that is easy to state and worth carrying into the investigation: an instrument is only invisible when its resistance is negligible compared with the circuit it is measuring, and the ratio in (c) and (d) is the quantitative form of that rule.

provenance.adaptation: Original cluster. Items (c) and (d) are paired deliberately so that voltmeter loading and ammeter insertion are seen as the same idea from two directions, and (a) and (b) are paired to separate recall of the maximum power condition from understanding of it.

verification.method: Each key and each distractor recomputed in Python to full precision, with every distractor confirmed to be exactly the output of the error named in its rationale.
solution_skeleton: model the non-ideal element by adding its resistance to the network
recompute the equivalent resistance of the circuit as modified
apply the potential divider or the power relation to the loaded circuit
compare the loaded result against the idealised value and match an option
